en: The Illuminating Lamp Commentary on the Guhyasamāja Tantra: An Explanation of the Six Points. Oṃ! Homage to Śrī Vajrasattva.

The glorious Sovereign of Tantras, the first chapter: That *Guhyasamāja* of the Jinas—which is easy to understand through the most clearly revealed Yoga Tantras, which is the domain of the Sons of the Victors bound by the six points, and which was obtained by the illustrious Nāgārjuna as the abode of the two stages and sealed by all the Buddhas—the Lord Candrakīrti reveals that pervasive Śrī Vajrasattva in due order.
First, there should be the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), which accomplishes the form of the mantra;
the second stage is said to be the mere contemplation of the mind (*cittanidhyapti*);
and the third, delightful stage is the vision of the truth of the conventional (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
The purification of conventional truth is called the fourth stage;
the fifth, known as "union" (yuganaddha), is this branch of practice which is the conjunction of the two truths and the summary of the meaning of all tantras.
He who knows the divisions of these sequences and their synthesis through the method of expansion (*prastāra*),
indeed knows the Tantra—
from the mantra, from the mind, from the body, from purity, and from the flow of the yugas.
Having gradually understood the meanings of the five clusters (*piṇḍa*), one should enter the six points (*ṣaṭkoṭi*).
Thus, as far as *ya-ra-la-va* ending with *ha*; *ka-kha-gha* ending with *cha*; *ca-jha* ending with *ṭa*; and *ḍa-ḍha-pa* ending with *ta*—these are rooted in the three syllables.

The second sequence: the six divisions are the mantras; the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma of the Great Sage are difficult to understand due to their seven ornaments, and therein they are bewildered—this is the Śrī-Samāja-karaṇḍa, and therefore it is the crest-jewel of that Tantra.
Since it is concise in its text yet vast in its meaning,
one should always exert effort to understand it through the grace of the Guru's feet.
Out of a desire to benefit sentient beings, I shall provide its classification:
the introduction consists of five parts, the logic is fourfold,
the commentary has six points, and the narrative is of four kinds.
The fifth has two divisions, the sixth possesses five divisions, and the seventh has two divisions; such, in brief, are the ornaments. For each of these seven ornaments, in their respective order:

I shall now provide an exposition according to the explanatory tantras (*vyākhyātantra*). What is the designation of this tantra? For what purpose was it composed? Who is the author? What is its authority? And what is its purpose?
The name of the tantra is its designation; the purpose is for the sake of passionate people.
Vajrasattva is proclaimed as its author; furthermore, it is fourfold in terms of its extent, its divisions, its chapters,
and its sections, both according to the text and by number.
The purpose, however, consists of mathematics, the eight supernatural attainments (*siddhis*), the ritual procedures for pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth,
and even supreme Buddhahood; thus, the second introductory section (*upodghāta*) is further explained.

Continuity, cause, etymological derivation, and reason—these are the terms for the arising of birth among humans. "Continuity" refers to [the state] from within the inner apartments; "cause" refers to the departure from the midst of the harem.

The *Guhyasamājatantra-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā* states: "Vow (*saṃvara*) is designated as discipline (*vinaya*), and etymology (*nirukti*) is proclaimed [as the means]. One who desires the fruit should practice the Dharma; that is called the cause.
This is held to be the fourfold method for the Dharma of detachment (*virāga*).
Now, in the system of the Dharma of passion (*rāga*), I shall explain the awakening to the clear meaning."
The arising from the five Buddha families is called the "lineage" (santāna); furthermore, becoming of a single family is shown as the "cause" (nidāna),
and the grasping of the vajra and so forth is called the "etymological explanation" (nirukti).
Furthermore, the third ornament is called *caryā*, which is the cause of the erotic and other aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*); it is the ascertainment of the six points (*ṣaṭkoṭi-pada*),
and it is designated as Yoga because it awakens the meaning that has been sealed.
Based on the distinction between intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*) and non-intentional language, and between the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) and the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*),
as well as literal and non-literal expression, it is proclaimed that there are six parameters (*ṣaṭkoṭi*).
The Jina speaks in an obscure manner and with interpretable meaning for the sake of those who are unfortunate.
Furthermore, that which is spoken for the sake of illuminating the reality of things as they truly are,

and which reveals the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatattva*) to beings of superior inclination by means of seemingly contradictory expressions— that is called "intentional speech" (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*).
For the sake of awakening sentient beings with dull faculties,

the very clear exposition of reality is explicitly stated as being without intentional ambiguity (*asandhi*) in the various ritual manuals for mandalas and so forth, as well as in the conduct (*caryā*), according to their respective requirements.
The explicit statement of meaning is that which is spoken according to the literal sense;
words such as *koṭa* and so forth, which are excluded from both worldly usage and the treatises,
are the conventions of the Tathāgatas— that is proclaimed as "not literal."
The sixfold division has been stated; now the different types of exegesis are being described:

the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*), the comprehensive meaning (*samastāṅga*), the embryonic meaning (*garbhī*), the ultimate meaning (*kōlika*), the concealed meaning (*pracchanna*), and the supreme meaning (*paramā*).
XLVIII. Regarding the *dhī*:
the first [type] is indeed single; the *samastāṅga* is of two kinds;
the *garbhin* is known to be threefold; and the *kolika* is considered to be twofold.

Many who know the external treatises are devoted solely to words; for the sake of clarifying their proficiency, the literal meaning is now being declared so that those who have entered into the Sūtras and other scriptures may be freed from remorse.

And through the yoga of the generation stage (utpattikrama), the complete set of limbs is revealed. It is called "Garbha" because it contains within it the revelation of the dharma of passion (rāga) and the discernment of the three knowledges of true awakening (satyasaṃbodhajñāna).
The concealed [meaning] consists of the luminous manifestation and the awakening to the unified state (*yuganaddha*);
these two types are declared to be the *kolika*. "Kola" signifies the ultimate limit.
The speaker who wishes to cause others to hear [the teaching] further divides it into two kinds.

The second is the explanation for disciples as taught in the *Satravyākhyāna*. One should apply the literal meaning (*yathāruta*), that which lacks intentional terminology (*asandhyā*), and the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
The "literal meaning" (*akṣarārtha*) is said to be the *Satravyākhyāna*, which consists of all the constituent parts.

The literal meaning (*nairukta*), the definitive meaning (*niyatārtha*), as well as the intentional terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*), the hidden (*garbha*), and the collective (*kolika*)— these are intended for the explanation for disciples; thus,
the different modes of explanation are demonstrated by relying upon the two stages (*krama*).

In accordance with the explanatory tantras, the Tathāgatas have taught that among those to be trained in the world, there are always five types of individuals recognized as seekers of hearing [the Dharma], due to their diverse mental dispositions arising from the nature of necessity.
The *ratnacandana*, the *padma*, the *puṇḍarīka*, and likewise the *utpala*—
these are by nature designated as distinct, yet they have been taught by the Omniscient One;
for one who is skilled in retention, there is no object whatsoever that remains unheard.
The person known as Utpala forgets [what he has learned] in an instant;

having heard much more that is worthy of being grasped from the *Guhyasamāja-tantra-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā*, the person named Puṇḍarīka is unable to manifest it further, like a water-jar filled with cotton.

One who possesses faith, compassion for people, and an expansive heart from hearing the teachings, is a person renowned as a "Lotus-like" individual; he receives the transmission like a jointless bamboo flute.
Conversely, one with little learning and great pride speaks much that is groundless.
It is not possible to bestow favor upon the person known as Candana,
who is virtuous, pure, skillful, wise, and single-minded;
having heard [the teaching], he would proclaim it correctly— he is renowned as a jewel-like person.
Puṇḍarīka, Utpala, Padma, and Candana—
these four are indeed the individuals (pudgala) who are persons capable of explaining the Satra;
and this one named Ratna-pudgala is fit for the yoga of the completion stage (niṣpannakrama), adorned with virtuous conduct.

The wise Vajrācārya, having examined whether a disciple is a fit or unfit vessel for exposition according to the distinctions in their knowledge of individuals, should provide two kinds of instruction.
By means of these six ornaments, the determination of the two truths is established;
indeed, this seventh ornament is the accomplishment of the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*).
This commentary, which follows the explanatory tantras (*vyākhyātantra*), has been declared to be very difficult to obtain.
For it is by this very method that the Yoga Tantras are led [to understanding], and not otherwise;
therefore, one should diligently uphold the Yoga Tantras from a Vajra Master who is proficient in the explanatory tantras through both the sequence of the introduction and the sequence of yoga.
Thus concludes the principle of the narrative concerning the sevenfold ornaments.
Now, the summary meaning of the seventeen chapters is set forth;
therein, Mahāvajradhara consists of both the signifier and the signified.

In the first chapter, having bestowed the *vidyābhiṣeka* upon those capable of hearing it within the *nirmāṇamaṇḍala*, he taught the practice of the *niṣpannakrama* (the stage of completion) by distinguishing between the provisional (*neyārtha*) and definitive (*nītārtha*) meanings— as set forth in the *Pradīpoddyotana* commentary on the *Pradīpodyotana-nāma-ṭīkā* (Pra0mā0), and as elucidated in the *Prakāśa* commentary on the *Pradīpodyotana* (pra0 bhāṣite)— in Chapter XLVIII of the *Pradīpodyotana*.

In the sixteenth chapter that is about to be explained, having reached another point, he describes precisely the yoga of the two types of deities; he states this matter in the *Samājottara*: "The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two sequences: the sequence of generation (*utpattikrama*) and the sequence of completion (*niṣpannakrama*)."
Thus,
in the second chapter of the *Guhyasamāja* (18.84), it illuminates the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*) alone.
In the third chapter, he clarifies the yoga of the completely pure deity;
in the fourth chapter, he reveals the initiation mandala.
In the fifth chapter, he teaches the practice of yoga;
in the sixth chapter, he teaches the empowerment of body, speech, and mind;
and in the seventh chapter, he elaborates upon the practice taught in the fifth chapter.
In the eighth chapter, he explains the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*);
in the ninth chapter, he explains the marvelous prophecy (*adbhutavyākaraṇa*);
and in the tenth chapter, he explains the external and internal exhortation of the heart of the deity for the purpose of bringing about the desired accomplishments (*abhimatasiddhi*).
In the eleventh chapter, he demonstrates the accomplishment of the mantra-body and the accomplishment of the gnosis-body;
in the twelfth chapter, he explains the transformation of the mahāmudrā;
and in the thirteenth and fourteenth chapters, he explains the expansion of ritual activity (*karmaprasara*).

In the fifteenth chapter, he teaches the illusion-like meditative absorption (*māyopama-samādhi*), stating that all accomplishments (*siddhi*) are achieved only by one who has realized reality (*tattva*).
In the sixteenth chapter, he elaborates upon the powder mandala (*rajo-maṇḍala*) described in the fourteenth chapter.
In the seventeenth chapter, he set forth the commitments (*samaya*) and vows (*saṃvara*).
Now, the division of the sixteen million words and the fourfold classification of the narrative for the seventeen chapters are being set forth.
From "Thus have I [heard]" up to "dwelt" constitutes the fourfold narrative.
From "Inexpressible," beginning with the assembly, up to "dwelt in the heart of the Bodhicittavajra," is of interpretable and definitive meaning.
The samādhi named Sarvatathāgatābhibhavanavajra, the samādhi named Jñānapradīparajovajra, and the samādhi named Kāyavākcittavisaṃvādanavajra; these are the fourfold narrative.

The meditative absorption named *Mahārāgavinaya* (Subduing Great Passion), the meditative absorption named *Samayodbhavavajra* (Vajra Arising from the Pledge), the meditative absorption named *Ratnasaṃbhavavajra* (Vajra Born of the Jewel), the meditative absorption named *Mahārāgasaṃbhavavajra* (Vajra Born of Great Passion), the meditative absorption named *Sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajra* (Vajra of the Passion of All Tathāgatas), the meditative absorption named *Rāgadharānurāgaṇavajra* (Vajra of the Passion of the Holder of Passion), the meditative absorption named *Vairocanavajra* (Vajra of Vairocana), the meditative absorption named *Sarvatathāgatābhisambodhivajra* (Vajra of the Complete Enlightenment of All Tathāgatas), the meditative absorption named *Dharmaratnākara* (Mine of the Jewel of Dharma), the meditative absorption named *Kāyavākcittavajra* (Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind), and the provisional and definitive meanings.

"The secret of body, speech, and mind," "the assembly," "by means of the words arising from the vajra-samaya," "the fourfold narrative," "the form of the Great Knowledge-Person," and "by the clouds of jewels of the samaya of the radiation of worship"— these are the interpretable and definitive meanings in the third chapter. The Illuminating Lamp Commentary on the Guhyasamāja Tantra: "Aha! Indeed, the activation of the bodhicitta of all Buddhas is the secret of all Tathāgatas; it is inconceivable and without abode"—this is not of intentional meaning (*nāsandhya*).
However, from the words "this causes even all the Tathāgatas to have doubt" up to "he does not dare to explain the secret of body, speech, and mind," this is intentional terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*).

From the words "in the family of hatred" up to "he caused him to sit at the northern gate," [the section] beginning with the emission of Vajrasattva and ending with the emission of the wrathful Amṛtakuṇḍali is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*),
[and is designated as] Vajradhṛk.

The mantra words beginning with "Prajñāntakṛt," "Padmāntakṛt," and "Vighnāntakṛt," up to the chapter on the empowerment of the samādhi-maṇḍala of all Tathāgatas, are of both interpretable and definitive meaning.

In the first chapter, the analysis of the six points (*ṣaṭkoṭipadavibhāga*): Now, from "the Blessed One," etc., up to "having understood their deliberations, he spoke to those Bodhisattvas," is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*). From "they should generate [it]," etc., up to "by means of the utterance of speech," is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*). "O, indeed, of Samantabhadra, the Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind..."
Through the practice of non-arising, this arising is proclaimed.
Up to this point, including the verse ending with *guhyasamāja* 2.2, there is no *saṃdhyābhāṣā*.
The passage beginning with "The non-existence of cultivation" (*abhāve bhāvanābhāva*) and so forth is the fourfold narrative consisting of the verses on the *bodhicitta* of Mahāvajradhara.
“Free from all entities, devoid of the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and the grasped and the grasper;

through the equality of the selflessness of phenomena, one’s own mind is primordially unarisen, its intrinsic nature being emptiness. Thus, beginning with these words and ending with “Homage to you, O Bodhicitta,” there is no intentional language (*saṃdhyā*).
The Second Chapter.

Now, from "Then the Blessed One" (*atha bhagavān*) and so forth, up to "I am of the nature of the *dharmadhātu-vajra*" (*oṃ dharmadhātu-vajra svabhāvātmako’ham*), is of interpretable and definitive meaning.

From "The great jewel of five colors" (*pañcavarṇa-mahāratna*) and so forth, up to "one should emanate, being of the nature of emanation" (*sphārayet spharaṇātmakaḥ*), is the fourfold narrative (*ākhyāyikā*). [This concludes] the *Guhyasamāja-mahātantra*.

"One should draw a moon mandala situated in the midst of the space-element," and so forth, up to the end of the chapter on meditative absorption titled "The Vajra Array.
This is of both interpretable and definitive meaning.
The Third Chapter.
The section beginning with "Then" and ending with "supplicated with the King of Praises" is to be taken literally (*yathāruta*).
The section beginning with "O you who are all Tathāgatas" and ending with "charioteer of the circle of sounds" is not in code (*nāsandhya*).
The section beginning with "Then, O Vajradhara" and ending with "the form of the mandala" is to be taken literally.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain... [and so forth] up to "...in the mind-maṇḍala of all the Tathāgatas"; this section is of both interpretable and definitive meaning. || The Fourth Chapter ||
The passage beginning with "Then" and ending with "the characteristics of conduct" is to be taken according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).
The passage beginning with "arisen from the non-conceptual object" and ending with "the unsurpassed Mahāyāna" is not of intentional meaning (*nāsandhya*).
The passage beginning with "outcastes" and ending with "those intent on reviling the master do not succeed in the practice" is to be taken according to the literal meaning.
The section beginning with "of those who take life" and ending with "they are indeed fit for the practice" is *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).
The section beginning with "mother and sister" and ending with "of the wise one free from conceptual construction" is of both provisional and definitive meaning (*neyanītārtha*).
The section beginning with "Then indeed" and ending with "this is the stage of the conduct of awakening" is according to the literal sense (*yathāruta*).
Now, the passage beginning with "indeed, ineffable" and ending with "became unconscious" is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
The passage beginning with "then, O Blessed Ones" and ending with "the bodhisattvas" is according to the literal sense (*yathāruta*).
The passage beginning with "then the Blessed One" and ending with "remained each upon their own seat" is of interpretable meaning.
From "Then," etc., until the end of the chapter titled "The Supreme Chapter on Universal Conduct" (samantacaryāgrapaṭala), there is no hidden meaning (nāsandhya).
|| The Fifth Chapter ||
The passage beginning with "Then" and ending with "characterized by the characteristics of mantra" is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
The passage beginning with "Then the Blessed One" and ending with "characterized by body, speech, and mind" is intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*).
The passage beginning with "Then the glorious Vajradhara" and ending with "the transgression of body, speech, and mind" is of both interpretable and definitive meaning (*neyanītārtha*).

The sixth chapter.
Now, from "Then the Blessed One" up to "attains accomplishment quickly," [the text] is to be taken according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).
From "one who subsists on alms" up to "one who enjoys all desires," it is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*). And the Buddhas...
The section beginning with "Thus, etc. and ending with "by the enjoyment of all desires" is the fourfold narrative (ākhyāyikā).
The section beginning with "by the conjunctions of the recollection of the Buddha," etc., and ending with "one shall attain enlightenment" is intentional language (saṃdhyābhāṣā).
The section beginning with "a sixteen-year-old," etc., and ending with "the delightful one" is non-intentional language (nāsaṃdhyam).
The section beginning with "recollection of the Buddha" (*buddhānusmṛti*) and ending with "the form of the mandala" (*maṇḍalākāra*) is intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*).
The section beginning with "how so? (*tat katham*) and ending with "may it be likewise for me" (*mamāpi tādṛśaṃ bhavet*) is literal (*yathāruta*).
Therein, the section beginning with "how so? and ending with "one would attain accomplishment most excellently" (*sutarāṃ siddhim āpnuyāt*) is intentional language.
In this regard, the section beginning with "How so? and ending with "perfectly pure" is not of intentional meaning (*nāsandhya*).
The section beginning with "In this regard, how so? and ending with "the chapter on conduct" (*caryāpaṭala*) is according to the literal sense (*yathāruta*).
The Seventh Chapter.
Now, from "Then the Blessed One" up to "O Supreme Victor, perform the worship of the place," it is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).
From "Passion, hatred, and great delusion" up to "Then the Blessed One" and so forth, ending with "equanimity does not abide anywhere," it is not of intentional meaning (*nāsandhya*).
From "Then the Blessed One" up to the end of that section, ending with "his life," it is according to the literal meaning.
Now, the passage beginning with "Then Vajradhara, the King" and ending with "the ocean of Jinas, the Bodhicitta" is *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).
|| The Tenth Chapter ||
Now, from "Then the Blessed One... up to "...the samādhi called Samayavajra" is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).
From "Mahāvajradhara... up to "...the samādhi called Candravajra" is intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*).
From "Situated in the center of the space-element (*khadhātu*)... up to "...the samādhi called Saṃbodhivajra" is not intentional language (*nāsandhya*).
The section beginning with "On the mountains" and ending with "the compendium of meditations" is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
The section beginning with "Akṣobhya" and ending with "conversant with the commitments" (*samayābhijña*) is according to the literal sense (*yathāruta*).
The section beginning with "the five-pronged [vajra]" and ending with "the chapter on the Knowledge-Person" (*vidyāpuruṣapaṭala*) is in the twilight language (*sandhyābhāṣā*).

Now, from "Then Vajradhara... up to "...this drama is to be visualized" is not of intentional language (*nāsandhya*).
From "The great forest... up to "...the compendium of all accomplishments" is of interpretable and definitive meaning (*neyanītārtha*).
From "Body, speech, and mind... up to "...with a radiance equal to Mañjuvajra" is intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*).
The section beginning with "by one's own mantra" and ending with "of the Gnosis-Vajra-holder" is to be understood according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).
The section beginning with "by the nectar of the gnosis of service" and ending with "the achiever of the reality-meaning of mantra" is *sandhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).

The passage beginning with "mahāṭavī" and ending with "samaśruta" is of both interpretable (neyārtha) and definitive (nītārtha) meaning. The passage beginning with "catuḥsandhyā" and ending with "dinabhedapracodanaiḥ" is according to the literal sense (yathāruta).
The statement, "Success is said to occur within two fortnights by those born of the supreme secret," is in the language of intentional terminology (sandhyābhāṣā).
In this regard, the section beginning with "tatredam" and ending with "sādhanāgranirdeśapaṭala" is to be understood according to the literal meaning.
|| The Twelfth Chapter ||
Now, from "Then the Blessed Ones... up to "...uttering the vajra-sound" is to be taken literally (*yathāruta*).
From "Aho! the Buddha-way... up to "...the mantra-way is firm" is *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).
From "In the unarisen... up to "...the arising of gnosis is proclaimed" is not *saṃdhyā* (it is literal).
"Speak, O Blessed One, the delightful compendium of all mantras," and so forth, up to "recitation is called neuter"—this is *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).
"O Lords of the Vajras," and so forth, up to "by those who serve according to their desire"—this is *yathāruta* (literal language).
"O pledge of delusion," and so forth, up to "of the practitioner who possesses the foremost dharma"—this is both *neyārtha* (interpretable meaning) and *nītārtha* (definitive meaning).
From "The vajra situated in the center of the heart" up to "is taught for the sake of protecting awakening" is to be taken literally (*yathāruta*).
From "Situated in the center of the space-vajra" up to "the samādhi named Illuminator of the Vajraratna Mantra" is *sandhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).
From "In all forms" up to "one may walk upon water" is to be taken literally.
The section beginning with "samayodake" and ending with "the samādhi named Vajrodadhipadākrānta" is in *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).
The section beginning with "māhendramaṇḍalam" and ending with "the samādhi named Vajrasumbhaprabhāvana" is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).
The section beginning with "nirodhakrodhavajreṇa" and ending with "they are accomplished from the vajra-maṇḍala" contains both interpretable (*neyārtha*) and definitive (*nītārtha*) meanings.

The thirteenth chapter.

In the fourteenth chapter, the garland-mantras and the extensions of ritual activities are presented according to their literal meaning; however, some among them are expressed in intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣita*). It is the same in the fifteenth chapter.

In the seventeenth chapter, some vajra-words are spoken in intentional language (*saṃdhyā-bhāṣita*), some are not spoken in intentional language (*na-saṃdhyā-bhāṣita*); some are according to the literal sound (*yathā-ruta*), some are not according to the literal sound (*na-yathā-ruta*); and some are of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), while others are of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Regarding these six categories of words, the Sūtra was taught by the Blessed One in the Explanatory Tantra (*vyākhyā-tantra*): "Intentional language and not intentional language, Interpretable meaning and not interpretable meaning, According to the literal sound and not according to the literal sound— This indeed is the sixfold point (*ṣaṭkoṭika*) of Yoga Tantra."

In this sequence, beginning from the *vijahāra-pada* (the place of sporting), the meaning of the *Śrī-samāja* is sealed by means of the exposition of the six points (*ṣaṭkoṭi*) and the fourfold exposition (*caturvidha*).

Failing to comprehend that, sentient beings who are attached to sense objects rely on the literal meaning of the words; having performed contradictory and extraordinary causal actions, they fall under the power of karma.

Thus, because of the statement in the *Saṃvara*, the commentary *Guhyasamāja-tantra-pradīpodyotana* [ends] with "Śrīvajrasattva is established in all space. Then, with the words beginning "Now, indeed, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya," he demonstrates the assumption of a nirmāṇakāya by entering into the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth for the sake of performing the welfare of sentient beings; this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
To illuminate that very point,
he says "atha" and so forth: the unification of the past, future, and present Tathāgatas through the sequence beginning with Candravajra is the "overpowering of all Tathāgatas."

For that purpose, he entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) named "Vajra" itself; immediately thereafter, as expressed by the phrase "he became," he came to exist as consisting of the vajras of all the Tathāgatas.
This means that the Great Vajra himself became the deities of the maṇḍala (*māṇḍaleya*).
He asks what was done by that mandala-member, the Great Vajradhara; [the text] says:

"All sentient beings were possessed by the possession of Śrī Vajrasattva; they attained the state of Vajrasattva (ai), and therefore it is said that they became possessors of bliss and mental well-being."

All the limbs— the aggregates and so forth, which are the nature of all the Tathāgatas— are overcome and unified by means of that meditative absorption (*samādhi*) through the form of conventional bodhicitta; because it is indivisible like a diamond (*vajra*), the name of that very absorption is "Vajra," and he has entered into that absorption.
"Immediately thereafter," and so forth;

"the entire realm of space" refers to the hollow space of the seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*). "The vajra of all Tathāgatas" means that the method-knowledge (*upāyajñāna*) became, or rather was, composed of that and had that as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"All sentient beings" refers to those such as the *sthāṇu* (stumps, etc.).
"By the empowerment of Vajrasattva" means that through the arising of the knowledge of skillful means, they became possessors of the bliss and mental well-being of all the Tathāgatas;

the meaning is that, having been melted by the fire of great passion (*mahārāga*) through the union of the two organs, they experienced the bliss of supreme joy (*paramānanda*). This is the "pregnant sense" (*garbha*).
All Tathāgatas are the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); their overcoming is their unification within ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). That itself is the "vajra" because it is indivisible;

he entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) named after that. Immediately upon entering that absorption, the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), which is the threefold emptiness (*śūnyatraya*), became the Vajra of all Tathāgatas—the universal emptiness—and he became identical with it, having its very nature.
Now, by the passage beginning with "as many as," he illuminates this very same meaning; this is the *kolika* (ultimate) explanation.

Having brought forth this Mahāvajradhara through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), he now speaks the words beginning with "atha" while demonstrating the forms of both the completely pure and the impure deities.
The vajra of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas is the three syllables; because it is not to be transgressed, it is itself the *samaya* (pledge). From that, *saṃbhavaḥ*—you have arisen.
Because it is indivisible, it is "vajra";
he has entered into meditative absorption;
[he is] the form of the Great Knowledge-Man.
The syllables of the mantra of Great Knowledge;
he whose human form was produced by them is the Mahāvidyāpuruṣamūrti.
He caused the empowerment of the mantras of all the Tathāgatas to be empowered.

The mantras of all the Tathāgatas are those beginning with the syllable *oṃ*. That which has its consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—that is, its ritual placement (*nyāsa*)—by means of these is so described. By this, the following would be implied:

By means of the method described in the *Sādhana*, through the sequence of the four yogas, he empowered himself as Mahāvajradhara, the embodiment of all mantras, up to the stage of the three beings (*trisattva*). "He was seen by those residing in all world-systems"—this is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).

The *samaya* (pledge) of the Vajra of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas is *prabhāsvara* (luminosity); that from which [the deity] arises or originates is "born from that. Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*) is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), and the person (*puruṣa*) is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).

The deity’s form in the shape of a person, produced from these two and endowed with all excellent aspects and so forth, is the "form of the Great Knowledge Person" (*mahāvidyāpuruṣamūrti*), namely Mahāvajradhara.
He then empowered the empowerment that is the empowerment of the mantras of all the Tathāgatas.
The intended meaning is that he has brought himself to completion as one composed of the atoms of all the Tathāgatas.
"Immediately thereafter," and so forth, is as explained previously;

"Then," and so forth.

Māmakī, who is the pledge of the passion of the Vajra-holder, having entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) focused upon her, [did so] according to the literal meaning.
"Dveṣarati" means attachment (*rati*) toward Akṣobhya, who is hatred (*dveṣa*); this is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Delight in the purification of the affliction of hatred is "delight in hatred" (dveṣarati);
this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
That very Vajradhara, having assumed the form of Māmakī, should sit in the southwestern corner.
Vairocana is all the Tathāgatas according to the literal meaning; Locanā is the Vajra of Attachment to that,
according to the literal meaning.
"Delight in delusion" means that Vairocana is delusion; delighting in him is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Delight in the purification of delusion is "delight in delusion" (*moharati*);
this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
One should sit in the southeast corner.
According to the literal meaning,
"atha" and so forth refers to Amitābha, the bearer of passion (*rāgadharah*).
Vajrā is the passion for that, and Pāṇḍaravāsinī is the meditative concentration (samādhi) having that as its object; thus it is said according to the literal meaning.
"Delight in passion" (*rāgarati*): "passion" (*rāga*) is Amitābha; "delight in him" is *rāgarati*; this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Delight in the purification of passion is "passion-delight" (*rāgarati*);
this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Then, and so forth, one should sit in the northwest corner.

Not taking [the words] literally, [it says]: "The commitment (*samaya*) is the passion-delight (*rāgarati*); there is no [other]. This is the *Guhyasamāja-tantra-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā*. Regarding the passage beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and so forth: "Deceiving the body, speech, and mind" (*kāyavākcittavisaṃvādana*) is the proclamation to others that the body, speech, and mind are impermanent.
The literal meaning is that "all phenomena are empty"; this is the objective support, while the deception of body, speech, and mind constitutes the complete set of factors.

Body, speech, and mind, which have the three appearances as their intrinsic nature, enter into their respective appearances from the subtle element, causing them to be experienced moment by moment; then, bringing about their lack of intrinsic nature is the "deception" of body, speech, and mind— this is the *garbha*.

The making non-manifest of the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and so forth, by means of the sequence of breaking through the grasping at them as a solid whole, is the non-deception of body, speech, and mind;
because it is indivisible, it is their vajra.
The meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that has that as its object is named "the Vajra of Non-deception of the Body, Speech, and Mind of All Tathāgatas."
Amoghasiddhi, the holder of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas,
together with his consort Vajrā— an emanation of Samayatārā— brought about one-pointedness of mind in that form; such is the meaning.
According to the literal meaning,
"Vajrarati" means that Vajra is Amoghasiddhi; delight in him is Vajrarati.
"Delight in vajra-wisdom" is of interpretable meaning; "vajra-delight" is of definitive meaning.
Then, and so forth; one should sit in the north, in the northeast corner,
according to the literal meaning.
These four goddesses are the companions;

for all the Tathāgatas who enter into union with them, the supreme accomplishment is produced. Thus, "supreme queen" refers to the sovereignty over desires, which is expressed by the term "supreme queen's accomplishment."
The connection is as follows: "Then," and so forth, according to the literal meaning, [he] emitted the wrathful one.
Vairocanavajra is one whose vajra has Vairocana as its very nature of consecration;
the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) having that as its object is called "Vairocanavajra.
That by which the mandala of all Tathāgatas is empowered—that is, brought to completion—is described in that way.
According to the literal meaning,
"Yamāntakṛt" means that the Blessed One, by means of the samādhi of great wrath, brings about the end— that is, destroys— Yama, which is hell; thus he is Yamāntakṛt.
The term *neyārtha* refers to the darkness of delusion, which is ignorance; it means that one brings about its end— that is, destroys it— by means of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Yamāntakṛt,
whose meaning is definitive,
sat at the eastern gate, as indicated by the words "Then," and so forth.
According to the literal meaning,
"atha" and so forth refers to the perfect awakening of all Tathāgatas, which is Ratnasaṃbhava.

The vajra in the crown of that Aparājita-krodha is the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) which has that as its object; it is named Abhisambodhivajra, which is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*),
and the perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*) of all Tathāgatas is the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*).
Taking that very vajra as the object of focus is the definitive meaning (nītārtha).
"Prajñāntakṛt" (the ender of wisdom) means that one destroys the afflictions through wisdom; this is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).

Wisdom whose nature is conceptual construction—he brings it to an end by entering into luminosity; thus he is "the one who brings wisdom to an end" (*prajñāntakṛt*). This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
"Then," and so forth.

"Vajrasamayasamtrāsanam" means the terrifying of the wicked by means of the vajra-commitments (*vajrasamaya*). Alternatively, it refers to not deceiving regarding that appearance—the vajra-delight (*vajrarati*). It is accomplished through the meditative absorption (*samādhi*). "Vajrasamayāḥ" refers to the worldly *ḍākinīs*; the terrifying of them is "vajrasamayasamtrāsanam."
He sat at the southern gate;
"atha" and so forth are according to the literal sound [of the text].
Having entered the meditative absorption named after Hayagrīva, whose lineage is that very Akāra which is Amitābha, the jewel of the Dharma; he...

The Jewel of Dharma is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*); it is luminous, and Hayagrīva has that very form as his source of origin. One who has entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) having that as its object is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

"Padmāntakṛt" (the Destroyer of the Lotus) means that, like a lotus unstained by water, he remains unstained by the afflictions (*kleśa*) and destroys them; this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).

The lotus is the womb (*yoni*), meaning the interior or center; because he produces—that is, generates—the bliss of supreme joy (*paramānanda*) by means of the union of the two organs within that [womb], he is called "the Maker of the End of the Lotus" (*padmāntakṛt*); this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Then, and so forth;
he sat down in the west according to the literal meaning.

The Blessed One Amoghasiddhi is the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas; he himself is the Vajra of that noble wrathful deity Amṛtakuṇḍalika, and the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which has him as its object is likewise so called—this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
The place of purification for the Vajras of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas is the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*).
Taking that as the object of focus, it is of definitive meaning (nītārtha) because it brings an end to obstacles.
"Vighnāntakṛt" (the destroyer of obstacles) is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), as it means he brings about the end— that is, the destruction— of obstacles; here,
"obstacles" refers to the four elements (*dhātu*).
Because they cause obstruction through the affliction of the body resulting from decline and increase,

he brings about their destruction by means of the arising of knowledge regarding the methods [to counter them]; thus, "Vighnāntakṛt" (the Destroyer of Obstructions) is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Then, and so forth;
he sat upon the northern side according to the literal meaning.
The pledge beings (*samayasattva*), who are the mandala pledge beings, exist for the purpose of pleasing the members of the mandala;
they are so called according to the literal meaning of the term because they destroy all obstacles.
In this manner, one should place [the deities] at the four gates;
starting from the eastern corner, one should place Acala and the others,
and starting from the eastern panel, one should place Maitreya and the others.
Outside the central mandala, beginning from the eastern corner, one should place Rūpavajrā and the others;
the rule regarding the seats and so forth for all of them has already been established in the *Sādhanopāyikā*, lest there be practice without a teacher.

Just as the deity-yoga and the mandala were fully demonstrated by the Blessed One elsewhere, so too here, just as the body-mandala consists of the arrangement of thirty-two deities, so also does the emission-mandala.
How is it understood that the body-maṇḍala itself must indeed consist of the arrangement of thirty-two deities?
This was explained by the Blessed One himself in the Explanatory Tantra (*vyākhyātantra*).
To ensure that the meaning is beyond doubt for the assembly, the source is introduced as follows:
"O Great Being, listen! Do not reflect with a distracted mind.

Within this body of the Vajrācārya, there resides the sequence of the *Kāryājinasthiti*. In the commentary (*ṭīkā*), the reading is *dharmaratnākara*. Having established [the text], [it says]: "The internal center does not exist" (this phrase is absent in manuscript *pra*). From the *Guhyasamājatantrapradīpodyotana-ṭīkā*: First, he is established by means of the Body-Vajra, which is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
He is established as the aggregate of sensation by means of Anurāgaṇavajra.
The Blessed One is established as the aggregate of perception by means of the speech-vajra;
he is established as the aggregate of mental formations by means of the vajra of all worship.
The Blessed One, established as the aggregate of consciousness, is the Mind-Vajra;
the earth element, consisting of flesh and so forth, is the Blessed Lady Locanā who resides there. The water element, consisting of blood and so forth, is the Blessed Lady Māmakī who resides there.
The fire element, consisting of heat, is established as the Blessed Lady Pāṇḍaravāsinī;
the wind element, consisting of impelling and so forth, is established as the Blessed Lady Tārā.
The Tathāgata Kṣitigarbha is his faculty of the two eyes;
the Tathāgata Vajrapāṇi is his faculty of the two lineages.
The Tathāgata Gaganagañja is the sense-faculty abiding in his nose;
the Tathāgata Lokeśvara is the sense-faculty abiding in his tongue.
The sense faculty abiding in the mind is the Tathāgata Mañjughoṣa;
however, that which is designated as the body is a mass composed of the four elements.
The Tathāgata Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin resides there,
as does the Tathāgata Samantabhadra within the body of all its joints.
The Tathāgata Maitreya is in all the sinews of the body; the Tathāgata Yamāntaka is at the base of the right arm, and the Tathāgata Aparājita is at the base of the left arm.
The Tathāgata Hayagrīva resides in the lotus of the face; the Tathāgata Amṛtakuṇḍalin resides in the secret place.
On the right arm stands that Tathāgata Acala;
likewise stands the Tathāgata Ṭakkirāja.

The Tathāgata Cakravartin stands upon his own head,
and the Tathāgata Sumbharāja stands beneath his feet.
And indeed, all the Tathāgatas reside within this very body; thus is described the bodily maṇḍala of the Vajrācārya.
All these perfectly awakened ones, the entire assembly of the Buddha-body, cause one to enter nirvāṇa through the vajra-constructed teaching.
"May you quickly attain nirvāṇa, O Blessed One; may you become one whose roots of virtue are fully ripened.
Therefore, all the Victors are established within the body of the Vajra Guru."
O Mahāsattva Amoghadarśaka, listen! From that time forth, you shall always be served with diligence by all sentient beings as their Guru.
Likewise, the great Bodhisattvas of unfailing vision and great renown, satisfied, joyful, and thrilled, bowed down and prostrated themselves before him.
Thus it is said in the *Vajramālā*:
"By this same principle, the arrangement of the thirty-two deities must also be performed in the painted mandala";
this is the meaning demonstrated even with reference to the introductory context (*nidāna*).
The meaning of the Tantra has been stated right there; the remainder would be incidental.
Thus [it is said].

In the *Guhyasamāja*, the secret of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, this is the chapter on the empowerment of the maṇḍala of meditative concentration of all Tathāgatas. Having observed and realized the secret of body, speech, and mind, this was composed as the *Guhyasamāja*. That in which there is the empowerment of the maṇḍala of meditative concentration is thus described as the "Chapter of All Tathāgatas.

Just as a cloth (*paṭa*) wards off disturbances such as gadflies and mosquitoes, so too this meaning of the tantra is like a cloth because it wards off disturbances such as afflictions, karma, and rebirth; therefore, it is called a "cloth" (*paṭa*).
It is called a *paṭala* because it is a collection of texts (*granthasamūha*) that takes up or grasps (*lāti gṛhṇāti*) that [subject matter].
The Explanation of the Six Points in the First Chapter of the *Pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā*. Amoghadarśaka:

[End of First Chapter]. Second Chapter. Having thus completed everything with the first chapter, he now speaks the second chapter on the Awakening Mind (*bodhicitta*) in order to illuminate the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*).
The connection of the passage beginning with "Then," and so forth, is as follows: having prostrated to the Blessed One, they spoke thus;
[the speaker is] Mahāvajradhara, the sovereign of body, speech, and mind.
Having performed worship to him and having prostrated, they entreat the Blessed One, saying, "Speak the unsurpassed thought of awakening (bodhicitta)"; this is the connection [of the text].
Because he is liberated from all obscurations, it is the essence.

It is "supreme" because it is the undifferentiated nature of the triad of body, speech, and mind; it is "secret" because, through the metaphorical designation of the effect upon the cause, it cannot be revealed to those who rely on the systems of ritual action and so forth; for this very reason, it is "unsurpassed."
Now, the connection [of the text] is that the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattvas with the words beginning "by the mind alone" (*cetasāiva*), thinking:

"If the Blessed One were to grant us the instruction on the Great Bodhicitta for the sake of accomplishing the form of the completely pure deity, then the purpose of the Great Beings would be fulfilled."
Having thus known the mental reflection with his own mind, he said according to the literal meaning:
"May you generate [the thought]," and so forth; that is, may you generate the *bodhicitta* by means of the nature of the indivisibility of the three vajras.
To the question "How so?", he says: "The mind by way of the form of the body" means by way of the form of the Body-Vajra;
"the body by way of the form of the mind" means by way of the form of the Mind-Vajra;
and "the mind by way of the utterance of speech" means that the utterance of speech is verbal expression.
The meaning is "by that speech-vajra.
Regarding the passage beginning with "then," etc.:
having joined and unified the body, speech, and mind with the form of space, which is the nature of emptiness.
This is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
To explain how they should "generate" and "accomplish" the mind-made body (*manomayadeha*), it says: "the mind in the form of a body."

The accomplishment of the body, which occurs when the threefold mind together with the subtle element assumes the form of the *saṃbhogika* body, must indeed be such that the body is [produced] by way of the aspect of the mind;
for there is nothing whatsoever other than the mind, and the mind [is produced] by way of verbal expression.
"Whatever verbal expression there is, let that very mind arise in that form"—
thus, with the words "body" and so forth, the body, speech, and mind are thus perfected in the form of space.
Having joined and unified [the mind] with the luminosity that has the nature of space, one should manifest oneself as Mahāvajradhara.
And it is said in the *Śrīvajramālā-mahāyogatantra*: "There is no other yoga equal to the three realms; it is the essence, one's own life."
He beholds his own city, radiant and composed of ten million elements.
Within the triple world, there is nothing more essential than one's own life; he who perceives the triple world as a dream regards his own life in that same way.
Thus it is said.
The reality whose form is the three realms bestows unity;
the state of empowerment is the application of non-arising.
Therefore, "arising" is luminosity, characterized by the assumption of the form of the pure deity; this is emergence.
This "arising" (utpāda) is that by which it is proclaimed and explained; thus, it is not of hidden meaning (*asandhya*).

Through the respective verses on the essence of enlightenment (*bodhicittagāthā*) of the six Tathāgatas, it illuminates this very samādhi, which is the perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*) of all Tathāgatas, characterized by the non-duality of the two truths.
Its "method" (naya) is the means for its direct realization;
that very [means] is called "vajra" because it is as indestructible as a diamond (vajra), referring to the meditative absorption (samādhi) which possesses it—
this is not a cryptic teaching (nāsandhya).
When all things, both stable and moving, are absent, there is an absence of cultivation (*bhāvanā*); because of the absence of that which is to be cultivated, cultivation is not truly cultivation.
Furthermore, that cultivation which pertains to what exists is not cultivation, because [the object] exists even without cultivation.
Thus, in this way, that entity which is joined with existence and non-existence would not exist;
therefore, the object of meditation (*bhāvya*), the meditator (*bhāvaka*), and the act of meditation (*bhāvanā*) are not perceived—
this is the literal meaning.

Having negated all phenomena through the distinctions of "superior" and so forth, there is the cultivation that "conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are empty"; the non-existence of that [cultivation] is due to its being a view characterized by attachment to emptiness.

To negate the sign (*nimitta*), it is said: "Cultivation is indeed not cultivation. Furthermore, even that cultivation which consists of attachment to the forms of cause and fruit is not at all tenable, because of the non-duality of cause and fruit.
In order to refute the [notion of] aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), he says: "The sense is as follows," and so forth.
Thus, even that fruit of aspiration which has an external form does not exist, because of the absence of any apprehension of the aspiration and so forth.
Therefore, the cultivation of the forms of external objects is not perceived and does not exist,
because it is entirely devoid of the nature of mind.

Regarding those things such as the aggregates (*skandha*) which are said to be non-existent: since that which has become the "mere mind" (*cittamātra*)— the state of being [realized] when they are absent— is not purified because it is eternally non-existent,
he speaks in order to refute conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
Cultivation is not cultivation at all;
even that cultivation of the form of a deity which is like an illusion and consists of conventional truth is not tenable,
because it is purified by the clear light.
Thus, the nature of conventional truth would not be an entity,
because it is non-different from the two truths;
therefore, cultivation— the cultivation of the non-dual aspect of the two truths— is not apprehended.
The meaning is that it is obtained with great difficulty;
as for the "non-existence" of the embryo— that is, the absence of cultivation within the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya)— it is because [that truth] is pure from the very beginning.
Even that cultivation which consists of conventional truth is not cultivated because it is unreal; in this manner, an entity consisting of the two truths would not be something to be cultivated,
since liberation occurs through the mere vision of the non-duality of the two truths.

Therefore, Mahāvajradhara— having spoken thus regarding how the attachment to "the meditator," "meditation," and "the object of meditation" is neither perceived nor exists for those who have attained the stage of the Union (yuganaddha)— taught the *kolika* [meaning] in the *Sthirabalapra* and the *Urvyādipra*.
There is no mind, no dream, and no all-pervasive [delusion].

By the phrase "because of its truth," the connection is as follows: "Then the Blessed One Vairocanavajra proclaimed," which refers to that very adherence [to the view] that "it is indeed the *prabhāsvara*. This is from the *Guhyasamāja-tantra-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā* [A].

The commitment (*samaya*) of all Tathāgatas consists in the universal manifestation of all aspects; that very [state] is the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), which is the vajra, and the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) focused upon it.

"All entities" (*sarvabhāva*) and so forth refers to being devoid of all entities that serve as the vessel of the world, and furthermore, being free from the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, as well as the subject and object of grasping. This selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is luminosity.
By that, there is the state of non-dual equality;

through that equality of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyasamatā*), the Tathāgata Vairocana declared that one’s own mind is primordially unarisen, possesses a body inseparable from the three vajras, has emptiness as its intrinsic nature, and is the domain of the eye alone— this is not of intentional meaning (*nāsandhya*).

The inexhaustible limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all Tathāgatas is itself the vajra; the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that has that as its object is called the "Inexhaustible Vajra of All Tathāgatas," [realizing] that "these phenomena are unarisen."
These external and internal entities are unproduced because they are luminous by nature;
therefore, neither do phenomena exist, nor does the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Since even their *dharmatā* does not exist due to the absence of phenomena (*dharma*),
for this very reason the Tathāgata Akṣobhya declared that this method of awakening— the means to awakening— is firm, essential, like space, characterized by selflessness, and luminous.
The phrase "not without a secret convention" (*nāsandhyam*) and so forth is to be connected in the same manner as before:
the selflessness of all Tathāgatas is the ultimate truth; that itself is the *vajra*, and the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which has that as its object is [the *vajrasattva*].

The selflessness of all Tathāgatas is the ultimate truth; that itself is the vajra, and the meditative absorption (samādhi) having that as its object is the meditative absorption named "Vajra of the Selflessness of All Tathāgatas. [They are called] "non-existent" because they are signless (nirnimitta); "all phenomena" (sarvadharma) refers to those with outflows (sāsrava) and those without outflows (anāsrava).

"Devoid of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*)," it is said; since phenomena themselves are not established, how could there be their characteristics? If one asks, "How then is the manifestation of the deity [possible]?"—it is because they are "arisen from the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). *Dharmanairātmya* is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); arisen from that through the process of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) are those "arisen from the selflessness of phenomena."
Ratnasambhava said, "By the power of the previous momentum."

Regarding the passage beginning with "nāsandhyam atha" and so forth: the lamp of the flame of gnosis (*jñānārciḥ-pradīpa*) is precisely that; what kind [of lamp] is it? It is one whose light is luminous (*prabhāsvara-āloka*).

That very [reality] is the vajra; the meditative concentration (samādhi) that has that as its object is called the "Vajra-Lamp of the Rays of Gnosis. Regarding phenomena—both conditioned and unconditioned—that have not arisen and are unborn, there is no existence, and thus there is no state of being an object of cultivation.
And there is no cultivation;
for cultivation also does not exist because of the absence of anything to be cultivated.
He explains how the yoga with the deity occurs: "by means of the union of the two terms, space and ground.
Space is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) and the ground is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*); their union is their becoming one.

The meaning is that by this application of the term "space," the state (*bhāva*)— which is the form of Mahāvajradhara— is proclaimed; according to this principle, the state is the embodiment of Mahāvajradhara.
"It is sung, it is told"— thus spoke the Tathāgata Amitābha; "not with intentional ambiguity" (*nāsandhyam*), and so forth— the connection is as before.
The vajra-concentration called "Overpowering All Tathāgatas": its meaning is analyzed as follows—
"all phenomena are luminous by nature."
"Nature and luminosity" means "naturally luminous";
nature is conventional truth,
and luminosity is ultimate truth.

External and internal entities have the nature of the two truths; therefore, [the sequence is as follows]: the primordial luminosity, the primordial vajra of existence, the primordial dharmas of luminosity.
Thus, being pure from the beginning and equal to space,
because of its utter purity, awakening is neither the form of a fruit nor the realization; rather,
it is the cause that brings about its attainment.
Amoghasiddhi stated that because there is no absence of non-difference between cause and fruit,
the thorough knowledge of this very non-difference of cause and fruit is the firm path to awakening; this was not spoken with intentional ambiguity (*nāsandhyam*).
Then, "atha khalu" and so forth:
the secret of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas is the mental body (*manomayadeha*);
its *dharmatā* is purity by way of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
The syllable of that [teaching] is a composition of sentences that illuminates that state;
having heard it, they were struck with wonder by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) and attained the marvelous by way of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
"Aho, the Buddha! is praise by way of the door of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).

"Aho, the Dharma! is by way of the door of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). "Aho, the teaching of the Dharma! praises it as the cause of the teaching of the Dharma, which illuminates the non-differentiated nature of the two truths;
its meaning is the pure reality, luminous.

Therefore, O Bodhicitta Mahāvajradhara, you who possess such distinguished qualities— whose purpose is pure and whose body is completely purified— to you, born from the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyasaṃbhūta*), that is, arisen from ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), homage!

The stage of completion of the Buddha’s enlightenment is that by which he brings disciples to maturity; thus, he is the fulfiller of the Buddha’s enlightenment. Because he transcends all conceptual construction, he is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).
Therefore, because you are without an object of perception due to being non-referential, "Homage to you, O Samantānālamba";
and because you are auspicious throughout both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, you are Samantabhadra.
Because he is the nature of all perfections, he is the "all-purpose" one;
because of the radiation of the mandala of deities, he is the "promoter of the thought of enlightenment";
and "enlightenment" (bodhi) is the ultimate truth.
That by which the conduct of awakening (*bodhicaryā*) is practiced and attained is conventional truth;
O Great Vajra, whose nature is the two truths— to you, [the essence of] mind and so forth, homage!
What is the nature of the mind? It is "tāthāgata," for a Tathāgata is one who has gone to suchness (tathatā); that which belongs to a Tathāgata is therefore "tāthāgata.
